title: 2026 09 03 FEC
machineSummary: The Reserve Bank’s Monetary Policy Committee defended its 25-basis-point OCR increase to 2.75%. The Governor said the gradual hike addresses 4.1% fuel-driven inflation while supporting growth. Debates focused on regional economic disparities, high youth unemployment, and the impact of the Middle East conflict on global commodity prices.

chunks.text: Good morning. Welcome to Zoom bank. Welcome, Governor. Colleagues, Karen, Paul, and I understand you've brought some additional members with you this morning. So I'll hand over to you, Governor, to make a statement on that. Thank you. Good morning, Morena, Chair and Committee.

It's good to be back here. So yesterday, the Monetary Policy Committee agreed by consensus to increase the OCR by 25 basis points to 2.75%. And as you know, inflation remains above target, reaching 4.1% in the June quarter because of higher fuel prices. If we take out the direct effect of fuel prices, inflation was at 2.9%. Monetary policy cannot offset the direct effects of higher fuel costs on headline inflation.

But what it can and should do is to prevent this shock from becoming persistent inflation. So with the OCR at an accommodative level, the Committee judges that a gradual removal of monetary stimulus is appropriate to return inflation to target while still supporting growth and employment.

And now we do expect growth to strengthen and broaden over the coming year as household income is supported by lower inflation, and we expect to see also better labor market outcomes. Thank you. I'll stop there. Thank you, Governor. I will start off with an opportunity with- Thank you. And thank you very much for that summary, and I think that cuts right to the quick of it, of how persistent this inflation is going to be.

Mm-hmm. And Governor, the MPC says inflation reached 4.1% largely because of those higher fuel prices, as you identified. How much of that inflation can higher New Zealand interest rates realistically achieve? You say it's not intended to do everything, but in setting this rise, what was the Bank's expectations?

Yeah. So we do expect to see, and we're seeing some indirect effects from those higher fuel prices. So there are lots of goods and services that use oil. We have transport, we have freight, we have fertilizers for food, and we do expect to see some of those indirect effects coming through over the coming quarters. And for us, it's really important to ensure that this doesn't become embedded, so inflation stays up around 4 or even 5% over the medium term. Because if we have that situation, well, then households' purchasing powers

will be eroded. So bringing inflation back towards 2%, we do expect this to take about a year. That will help in terms of households getting the purchasing power back, and that will help job creation as well, because domestic demand is the weak part of the economy, and the exporting sector are doing better.

So thank you, and it's useful. What specific evidence did you look at when coming to this decision that shows that underlying domestic inflation is strong enough to require those higher borrowing costs if you strip out the fuel shocks- Yeah... essentially?

So there is a range of data that we look at. Of course, core inflation went up from... The median across different measures of core inflation was 2.4%. It's now up at 2.7%, so we've seen that going up. We do expect that to continue increasing somewhat over the coming months.

We expect to see more of those indirect effects coming through. And then now we've seen that inflation expectations have been coming down, but they've been uncomfortably high for a while, particularly on the shorter end, and we know that that tends to translate into firms passing on costs.

And we've also looked at producer prices, and they have also been relatively high and actually going up. So the cost pressures for firms are there. And what we would like to see is that the firms, to an extent that they can, really look through those higher cost increases, because expecting that inflation will come down, because that means that we will not have to tighten so much if firms try to hold back a little bit. So those are...

I don't know, maybe- Yeah. Thank you... Paul or Karen would like to add a bit. Yeah, that's headline inflation, excluding vehicle fuel increases. Which inclusive is at 4.1, excluding that it was at 2.9. Now, that's uncomfortably high-... relative to the midpoint of the target, and that would indicate to you that there are indirect effects that are translating through, and it is higher than, for example, we saw in February, so pre the crisis.

And our expectation of where it would be pre the crisis as well. So there are signs there that it is definitely having some impact. Cool. Thank you. And I think the report paints a picture that New Zealanders are feeling. It's a pretty bleak picture.

Mm-hmm. High unemployment, subdued wage growth- Yeah... falling real wages, weak household spending, job insecurity, and a cost of living that everybody is really feeling. So I guess the question is, what data, looking forward, what data will the Committee be looking for to conclude that the inflation shock is proving temporary, that domestic demand is too weak, and no further OCR rises are going to be required? What will be the critical data sets?

So first of all, we are saying that we're seeing a recovery, but it's uneven. So we are seeing some really good signs in the New Zealand economy right now, and particularly related to export. They've been considerably stronger than expected, and it's not a good environment out there, and exporters are also hit by higher fuel prices. So clearly there is competitiveness in the agricultural sector, the tourism, manufacturing. Not all, we know that, but many firms are doing rather well.

Mm-hmm. What we're seeing is that they are not hiring so much yet. They're more using hours. Mm-hmm. We can see that in the data. But what we're looking for now, and we're starting to see signs from, is that the export-led growth is starting to spread to other parts of the economy. We see that particularly with business investments.

So I just want to be clear that we see an uneven recovery, and we expect it to broaden. And then with the OCR, it's really important to understand that we're not on a preset course. Mm. So we're saying that at 275, that in historical comparisons is still relatively low. So we assess that this is good to bring inflation down, but it's still supporting growth and jobs.

So if you look at the forward-looking OCR track, there is a probability of another rate hike, but we also said that now after having done two OCR increases, we can probably take some time to assess and see how this has affected the economy and whether we see stronger or less strong second-round effects from the high fuel prices.

Can I just answer your question on the data? Yeah. We look at all of it, and we wish there was more of it for us to look at as well. In terms of medium-term inflation pressures and our expectations, as key price setting behavior is key. As the Governor said, there's nothing we can do about that near-term inflation pressure from higher oil prices.

But what we can and what we will do is stop that from morphing into generalized inflation pressure. So those indicators of medium-term inflation pressure are quite key, and this delicate balance that monetary policy is trying to pull off at the moment-... between supporting growth and preventing the price shock from becoming generalized inflation.

Yeah. Just honing in on how most people are See the economy, it's how they're experiencing it. It's high unemployment, it's subdued wage growth, it's falling real wages, it's weak household spending. It's all of those indicators that show that everyday New Zealanders are still feeling this in terms of those considerations.

And you talked, Governor, quite correctly about this being uneven. We know from in your report points to Auckland and Wellington- Yes... feeling this- Not the South Island. No, the South Island's always fine, as you know. But it's not, but it is uneven. But it's not just geographical, it's across different demographics, particularly young people as well.

Yeah. How concerning for you is this uneven pattern, and how do you see the rate rise impacting on that unevenness? I can start, and I'd be happy to let my colleagues comment as well. But the thing that we've seen is, yes, it is uneven, but we expect it to broaden, and we fully understand that many households are not feeling the effects of the fact that we are starting to be in a broader recovery yet.

The other thing is that we have discussed to what extent is this what we call business cycle, and to what extent is this more structural. So for example, take youth unemployment, that we know is high, we know that's a concern. We discuss things like, we see this in some other countries as well, is it possibly because firms are investing more in new technologies, and then it gets more difficult for younger people to come in to the labor market?

And this is a difficult question. There's a difference between what monetary policy can do and not do in this space. But actually, we see quite a few structural changes in the economy right now, and we find them important. But monetary policy is more effective when it comes to the business cycle. I'm happy to let Paul- I'd like a chip in, Governor. So low inflation, which is our primary mandate and our primary objective, we will support the rebalancing of the New Zealand economy. It will support that growth in the export sector to

spread across the rest of the economy. And I'll go back to my earlier comments. It's a delicate balance in the New Zealand economy currently. There's a lot going on. There's an oil shock working its way through a lopsided economy. As the Governor said, we've got technology nibbling away at different parts of the labor market. So it's a very complex picture, and lots of structural changes happening as well. And just to be very clear, our role is to get inflation down. That's what we can do with monetary policy.

And it's a blunt tool, but the rest of it is beyond the capability of monetary policy to address its context. Just very quickly on that, having a mandate that allowed you to look at things other than just inflation, for example, unemployment, would that have altered the decision?

That's a hypothetical. We spend a lot of time- On the labor market... Yeah. The labor market is still in there. It's a matter of the degree to which you want to incorporate it into our decisions in terms of the mandate. I do think normally in a demand shock, the effect is the same on inflation, on the labor market. It's a little clearer for monetary policy, and the breadth of the mandate doesn't matter so much.

It does become more delicate currently when we've got inflation going up and growth has been lackluster because of the shock. So picking our way through that, I think the mandate would, at the margin, have an effect. I can't say whether or not it would've altered the decision yesterday because we didn't do the process with a dual mandate in our minds.

The other thing we also need to just remember is that we're talking about a gradual withdrawal of stimulus. We are not talking about being in a restrictive environment. We're talking about stimulus still existing today, and that is all about supporting the recovery of the economy.

And as Paul said, trying to tread that fine line between ensuring inflation doesn't get away, which will destroy the purchasing power for all households, and ensuring that the economy still has sufficient condition available in order to see that movement beyond the export sector into the broader economy.

Thank you. That's the balance that we're trying to do. We're going to go now to Dan Bigwa. Thank you, Mr. Chair. Thank you to your team and to your fellow MPC members for being here today. Just continuing on the theme of the report, the special topic around Iran. So what I took from that, if I can summarize, is that from the June CPI data, the indirect and direct effects accounted for two-thirds of the inflationary effect. Can I confirm that with yourselves?
Yes. So this is in the... We would have to look exactly on the pages here. It's on page 34- 34... of the monetary policy report. And

CPI was at 4.1%, and we do believe that the direct effect of higher fuel prices contribute to a large share of that. Then it's always difficult when we try to say how much of that is the direct effect, and then there's also some of those indirect effect, and we have to make some assumptions around them, transport costs, et cetera.

So I'd have to read carefully to ensure if I can exactly confirm your number. But what I said is that we believe that without the fuel cost, annual CPI inflation would've been more like 2.9%, which is still well above the midpoint of the target range. And some of that would include some indirect effects from the fuel prices as well.

Yeah. So certainly page 35, I take it that out of the 1.5% June quarter CPI, that essentially one percentage point of that is accounted for, which is roughly- Yeah... two thirds, so. Yeah. So in terms of the decision that was made yesterday, can I confirm the consensus of all members was to increase? Is that correct?

Yes, that's correct. Okay. You've come before us in the past saying with this crisis, there will be a certain view to look through this Iran situation. Yes. It's continued a lot longer than particularly anticipated. If core inflation continues to decrease- Core inflation's increased... it decreases... yeah.

Yeah. What factors will you consider in terms of continuing to look through it or holding or potential rate rises in the future? No, so I think the main thing is that we always look to all factors that affect inflation, and this is a complex process. So currently we've been looking at how much is inflation affected by the fuel prices, how much are indirect effects, and do we also see second round effects, which is more inflation expectations.

Do we see that the wage formation is not functioning as normal because of this? And then of course, how is demand in the economy? Because that will also affect inflation over the medium term. So, we will be looking at a wide range of factor, not just one or two factors.

What we've seen is, and that's what you're saying is because the conflict is Continuing. We know that it's still very tense in the Middle East. That means now that the fuel prices are staying at a high level, not at its peak, but still at a high level. And we see some risk then that that will cause more indirect effects than we thought a few months ago.

In May, it was looking considerably better, but we knew that there were risks at that time that it could flare up again. Yeah. It is right now. Yes. But then you've been engaging across the country with different stakeholder groups. Any views around what's doing well? We hear it's doing well.

What is that good news stories that you can see when you're out there engaging with different sector groups? Well, we have been engaging. I have a list somewhere of all the different places we've been to, and I do think it's remarkable the way that the business sector is working through this period.

And we're seeing high demand for New Zealand exports. And I think there are two factors, the fact that they are competitive, again, cultural sector is competitive, commodity prices are relatively high. But also that they're being flexible in terms of finding new export markets.

And then there are still some firms that are struggling more, and they're mainly related to domestic demand. Mm-hmm. And that is why we keep on saying, and Karen also just pointed it out, that getting inflation down will help those small businesses because we know then that households will start spending more, and that will flow through.

So currently, and we have that in the report, total disposable income is actually growing more than spending, so households are saving. Mm-hmm. There's a graph on that somewhere in the report. And it's not strange that households are doing some precautionary saving in this environment, but that also means that there's an upside.

Mm-hmm. When they see that the economy starts growing- Mm-hmm... they feel less job insecurity. Mm-hmm. We do see inwards migration. We see people moving across different parts of New Zealand to find jobs. That will help this adjustment, and that means that we can also see the household consumption growth starting more strongly again.

And what's the bank seeing in Auckland? It has been a particularly hard time in Auckland with elevated employ- Yeah. Yeah... unemployment. But confidence indices seem to be improving. What is the bank seeing with respect to Auckland? So that's true. We highlight both in terms of house prices and unemployment. Unemployment is higher in Auckland than it is in some other parts of the country.

It's probably related somewhat to youth unemployment. A lot of students, et cetera, are looking for a job, finding it more challenging in that environment. It's also probably related to the fact that house prices have been important for household wealth, and house prices haven't really rebounded in Auckland yet.

Mm-hmm. So we're discussing this, and there is an in-depth here talking a bit more about household consumption. And also, unfortunately there we don't have great data across the country, but we have some indicators of what is affecting that. I don't know, maybe Paul you'd like to add. Oh, I think you've nailed it, actually.

I think Auckland, times are challenging in Auckland. Unemployment, it's quite unusual to see a difference in unemployment above 6% in Auckland versus 4% in the South Island. So there are regional differences are quite extreme at the moment. Essentially because the South Island and parts of the North Island are more locked into, I don't know if booming is the right word, but an export sector that is going very well. Thank goodness, because that's the sort of growth engine in the economy at the moment. But it's a long way from Invercargill to Auckland for those effects

to make their way through the economy and through the geography. Just a bit on that topic. Mm. The regionalism. Mm. Is there a risk that Auckland, if we take it by itself, either is in recession or will fall into recession? I think it's like interest rates in Auckland, we've got one tool, we've got one currency, we set it for the whole country. It's a weighted average of economic conditions across the country. And this is part of the challenge for monetary policy at the moment is this idea of different parts of the country performing very differently.

But it's growth in Auckland going backwards. We don't have exact regional data. Sometimes we get regional data, but it tends to be more lag than GDP data. So currently we have GDP for the whole country only for the first quarter. We're still waiting for the second quarter data- Yeah... which we expect to look rather weak. But we are in the third quarter already.

We are in the September quarter where we think that things have actually started to recover. So getting that kind of regional data for the whole economy will take even longer is my understanding. But that's why we did look at some other measures like unemployment, like the house prices. I do think that we will see when we see the broadening of the recovery, that also some of those areas will start performing better.

And some of the things you look at there are the surveys that are occurring, right? Yeah. And are we starting to see a little bit more confidence- Confidence returning... returning in business and households? And certainly from a business perspective, those confidence surveys are showing a small uptick as well. So you're starting to see, but that's right at the very start of it. That then needs to translate into activity.

But certainly the surveys that are being done are starting to show more confidence around forward-looking orders and even past activity from a business perspective. So yes, while there might still be some divergence, there are some signs that things are starting to pick up in aggregate a bit more. But as been pointed out, there are distributional differences and issues there, and that takes time to change and move.

And there will always be a lag. And GDP growth was 0.8 in Q1. Yeah. Which wasn't too bad in the global context of what's going on. And yes, a lot of it was coming out of the export sector. Yes. But there is growth in this economy. It just seems that every Q2, this year it's conflict in the Middle East, last year it was tariffs- Mm-hmm... and all the uncertainties associated with that.

But in between, we grow, and we can grow. And this decision out of the committee yesterday is not standing in the way of that. Mm-hmm. It's supporting growth in the economy and employment. But it's calibrated to reduce those second-round inflationary effects through expectations and through pricing behavior of businesses.

Thank you. But it's a very delicate balance. I've been very patient, Mr. Chair, so I'd just like the spot that I was requested a few minutes ago into my primary one. Invitation. So actually, it trembles quite well off of that final point, which is just you've noted, obviously, commodity prices, I think we're all aware that's part of the reason that we're seeing this kind of K-shaped differential between North and South Island. The commodity prices, we're kind of lucky because of its price.

So if high commodity prices weren't being experienced internationally, and therefore that we wouldn't see that benefit our export markets, what would the impact be on our economy right now? Because I guess what I'm trying to get a handle on is the things that we actually have control over domestically versus those international things. Yeah. No, but I think that if we look at the commodity prices, New Zealand has been very negatively affected by the oil price.

Mm-hmm. And that is also part of that. So first we had in terms of trade, actually looking worse. And now when we see that oil prices, I will not use the word stabilized unfortunately, but they're highly volatile still. Mm. But we've seen the other commodity prices that are good for New Zealand, dairy, meat, these kind of things being high.

But we also know that the sector is competitive, fundamentally competitive. Mm. So this has just made, if you look at the exporting numbers, they're extremely strong right now. So I think if we saw a very strong reversal, of course that would be difficult. Mm. But this sector is so competitive that they could take softening of those very strong commodity prices.

I think the other point there, Chloe There is an element of good fortune in the fact that commodity prices are high for the things that we're good at currently. But also, the long-term trend in New Zealand's terms of trade- Mm... is pretty positive, actually. So we are quite good at shifting resources into industries and sectors that do end up getting, where global prices do tend to increase more than import prices. Now if I may just- And sorry, can I just say monetary policy does have an influence there through the

exchange rate. Yes, exactly. Yes. So we can't ignore that either. Totally. Yeah. Now I just want to explore some of the logic of this decision and then the implications of it, bearing in mind, as you two in particular well know, I'm very aware of the blunt instrument that is monetary policy. So I guess just lay out a few premises for the sake of continuing to explore this.

Firstly, just to be really clear, as you said in your opening statement, 4.1% inflation is largely being driven by, or it's outside the target band by virtue of the fossil fuel crisis, Trump's war on Iran. Yes? Headlines. Yes. It's called headlines, yeah. We know that monetary policy cannot reopen the Strait of Hormuz. It cannot decarbonize our economy and reduce our exposure to imported fossil fuel inflation. We accept that premise. Cool.

Yes. So only fiscal policy can do those things. Fiscal policy can open the Strait of Hormuz. No, but it could decarbonize our economy. It could invest in renewable energy and substitutes, either could. Those are choices of the elected officials. Thank you very much for making that explicit. So just to that effect, I just really want to understand, because many people out there will be saying, out in regular people land, whereby I completely understand you guys don't have the same platform or the freedom of politicians to unpack this

stuff, so I really would love to give you the opportunity to explain how monetary policy is a blunt instrument, but you are largely compelled by virtue of your enabling legislation to act when inflation is outside of the target band, but you can't actually deal with those structural fundamentals of the economy. Sure. We can deal with the indirect effects.

Yes. And we've seen that. We had a few years back a similar situation, it was very different in many ways. Mm-hmm. But what happened- It was all in committee. Yeah. So what we've seen is that monetary policy is really important in terms of containing the indirect and second-round effects of things like supply-side shocks.

Mm-hmm. And it does matter a lot for inflation expectations, for how core inflation evolves, and over the medium term, that turns out to be headline inflation. And what we're seeing right now is that there's a risk that unless we respond in monetary policy, those inflation expectations will get out of hand, and we will see a lot of firms taking the opportunity to hike prices in this environment.

Yes. Right. And we are seeing both some bad examples, but some also good examples of firms showing restraint, because then we will get back to inflation at a low and stable level more quickly, and that would really benefit everyone. But this will not happen without us doing anything.

No. So just thank you. I really appreciate you outlining that rationale. So to your point of inflationary expectations and price setting behavior, to make that really concrete for, again, real people outside of this space who don't necessarily understand this economic terminology, what you're talking about there is effectively, for lack of better terms, the animal spirit of the economy, whereby you have firms that can see that there is inflationary pressure, and they therefore can respond by setting prices at a certain level, which can arguably be justified,

and consumers will just accept it because there is high inflation. Is that effectively what we're talking about? Well, so look, firms are also hurt by higher costs presently. Totally. Yeah. So we have to allow for this, and I understand, I think it's really good to try to explain it in a sense and not use so much of the too complicated economic language, but some firms are hurting from higher costs.

Mm-hmm. And they're looking at, how can I survive in this environment? And their margins are small. Yes. Then there are other firms who fuel costs are not a big part of their cost structure, but they might still use this as an excuse to hike prices anyways. Yep. And for us, the balance is to try to make sure that we don't see the opportunistic price setting behavior bringing inflation back, because it will be better for everyone of the medium term.

And we're trying to take a balanced approach, and what we pointed out here is that we're coming from a relatively low level- Mm-hmm... at 2.25, and 2.5, 2.75 is still what we call accommodative, which is a technical term, but is saying that we think it's a level that's consistent with still supporting growth and jobs.

100%. Thank you for pointing out those differences and that some may take that opportunistic approach, because I think that that is a really important thing to understand, also monetary policy, obviously a blunt instrument. So we know that a higher OCR has the impact of contracting spending. It's the correlation there. Which then tends to correlate with higher unemployment.

Yes? The restrictive OCR- Well, it depends on where you're coming from Yeah. So we're coming from a level where the OCR is below what we think is restrictive, so we think is actually stimulatory. So what we're doing now, because the monetary policy transmission, and this is again, a technical term, it goes through a number of different steps.

Mm-hmm. So one is having an effect on wholesale interest rates, one is having an effect on household and firms' expectation, and one is an effect on potentially dampening demand. Currently, the main effects will be through wholesale interest rates, exchange rate, and expectations, not so much on dampening demand, because we're coming from a low level.

Last question. You've had your 10 minutes. Okay. So I guess to try and bring this all together, you noted at page eight of your report that growth and activity may not flow through into additional employment as expected, particularly if businesses are relatively more focused on efficiency and technology investment.

To that effect, we are currently going through quite a substantive industrial revolution, albeit lightly with the likes of AI tools being deployed and otherwise. So, you guys have very blunt tools at your disposal, typically, by releasing more expenditure into the economy, we then see growth and then that tends to, historically at least, result in higher growth, which then spills over into higher wages, more employment and otherwise.

But this to me seems like quite a stark warning that we might not necessarily see that recovery occur in that same way. Can you unpack for us what that actually means for the economy and potentially the efficacy of the tools at your disposal? Yeah, so this sentence is related to the record of the meetings, and we were talking about different kinds of risks.

Mm-hmm. So of course, there is a large upside potential of firms investing in new technologies. Mm-hmm. Creating productivity gains that tend to increase incomes. And what we've seen historically is that they tend also to create actually more jobs. Mm-hmm. What we're considering now is what we mentioned before, we're seeing youth unemployment in particular being high.

And there is a discussion here and in other countries, are firms a bit more reluctant to employing younger people because they might be able to use some tools? And we don't have a clear answer on this because no one actually can tell you with certainty. No. But we are saying that we're watching this, we're trying to analyze it.

We'll keep an eye on it. We don't think it's going to be an issue over the... We use the word medium term quite often because it tends to give much better incomes, so you can hire more people. But in the near term, we're wondering if it may have an impact, particularly on younger people. I think we've used that a short term in the- We'll ask them that question at the right times.

Sorry? Thank you. All right. I'll go to Nancy Lo. Thank you. I have three short questions. Firstly, welcome to the external members as well. I understand that all three of the external members are here. Yes. Yes. Is there a particular reason or would they like to share something on what they consider, too? So we discussed this, and we would be happy to.

We offered a bigger table again, but we think a nice way of doing it is that we can have the external members come up and answer questions. And Paul offered to- I'm very happy to rotate a little bit. So we have Prasanna Gagaik, Hayley Gourley, and Carl Hansen here. So they're happy to answer questions as well.

Yeah. So then my question to the external members would be when you went into the meeting- Did you all go in with your, I guess, your preference to vote for an increase already, or was that a more in-depth conversation with them? Yeah. Polly, want to start with that? We don't want Andrew to answer, but- Yeah. Thank you for the question.

As you can imagine, even in between meetings, even though this is not my full-time job, in between meetings, I try to keep an eye on what's happening in the economy and globally. And so one does tend to get an inkling and start thinking about things. But I certainly find that once we get the material from the Reserve Bank, which is very comprehensive, it really updates you, and at that point, we go to the first day or two, and we're getting staff presentations.

We get an opportunity to clarify what we're reading, and it's really at the end of that stage that we start putting quite a bit of thought to what we think we're going to recommend as individuals. Okay. Because the staff material includes the modeling and the forecasting-... which we don't get from just reading the general news in media.

That's a good point to understand. I always find that it's very instructive to get the material from the staff. And it's also very interesting to find out what the other members are thinking. So we talk about those things in a very structured way. We all form our own views, and then we go through a structured approach of what each of us are thinking about, so that we're keeping independence- Okay... and not falling into a group think kind of way.

Now, coming back to the governor- Mm-hmm... apart from learning in discussions within the inside, obviously, we're also looking at what the other countries are doing. And as noted, for example, in Australia, the OCR at the moment is at 4.35%. Looking into the UK, which is another area that we look into, is also quite high. However, the inflation rates in both these two countries are quite different.

What is your learning from the other countries? Because we all go through the oil crisis together. Yeah, and it's different starting points- Mm... and different structures in the economy. So we do look a lot at what's happening in other countries, both because they are important as export markets for us, but also because it can have implications, for example, for the exchange rate.

Yeah. It tends to be a relative- Yeah... feature. So we look at that. We know that, for example, in Australia, their economy was... I'm trying to be careful with the words I use. But they had high growth and low unemployment, so they were sort of hiking already before- Yeah... the oil prices hit and affected them as well.

So they're up at a considerably higher level than we are. And then it differs, and we need to look at each country is different, and I'm certain, talking to some of these other governors, that they focus on doing what's right for their country, and we're focusing on doing what's right for New Zealanders. And people are reacting differently, so, and economies, you're right, are different.

It depends on the energy intensity of an economy as well, and some are net exporters. Mm-hmm. And so that's a very different proposition to the one that we would face here in New Zealand. And some of them are adopting different fiscal approach to it as well. So you see subsidies in some economies, but that's a trade-off too.

Yes. What does that mean from a fiscal deficit perspective as well? Thank you. Thank you, members. I've just the time, got to keep moving. Dr. David. Yeah, just a little something, thank you, Nancy- Sure... for your question. With the international comparators, it's quite instructive, isn't it? I just wondered, we're looking at inflation, OCR, we mentioned the exchange rate as something. Paul was talking about terms of trade.

Yeah. All those factors are really- Factors... important for us, aren't they? One I'd chuck in there is the cost of capital and respective comparators. How do we line up there? Mm-hmm. So this is the question that is maybe more for when we're here for financial stability and these kind of questions, but we look at it from the perspective in terms of how well the transmission of monetary policy is functioning.
